Each label applied, overridden or re-adjudicated is attributed to an annotator and the guideline revision then in force.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the lineage map held for a sampled released model version.
Collect the records emitted by one full pipeline run, with digests per job and provenance per document batch.
Gather the append-only storage configuration, the hash chain and the denied tamper attempt.
Retrieve the labelling ledger for the period and the reconciliation write-up.

Analysis:
Walk the lineage from the released artefact back to an ingested corpus and note where the chain breaks.
Recompute one job's output digest and compare it with the lineage record written for that job.
Attempt to alter a stored model-change entry and confirm the write was refused and the attempt recorded.
Verify ledger entries name the annotator and the guideline revision current when the label was applied.

Output:
A lineage trace for the sampled version naming each missing entry and the stage that owed it.
A digest comparison result across the sampled pipeline run.
An immutability test record holding the denial captured and the hash chain checked.

title.en: Trace each deployed model version back to its datasets, transformation jobs and ingested corpora

description.en: Nobody can audit a trail whose shape is unknown. Take the model versions currently serving traffic and walk backwards through every training and fine-tuning run to the raw datasets, the jobs that reshaped them, the label batches applied and the document corpora ingested for retrieval. Mark each hop where the pipeline writes no record today: those breaks are what turn a later provenance question into a shrug rather than an answer. The map, with the breaks marked on it, is what this task hands over.

evidenceHint.en: Per-model lineage map naming every upstream dataset, job and corpus, with the unrecorded hops marked

text.en: List the model versions currently serving production traffic.
Walk each version back through its training and fine-tuning runs.
Name the datasets, transformation jobs and label batches behind each run.
Add the document corpora ingested for retrieval alongside each model.
Mark every hop where the pipeline writes no record today.

title.en: Write a lineage record at every transformation and a source tag on every ingested document

description.en: A pipeline that reshapes data silently leaves the organisation reconstructing provenance from memory months afterwards. Make each transformation job emit its input and output digests, the code version that ran and the parameters it ran with, and make the ingestion path stamp every document with where it came from, when it was fetched, under what licence and the checksum of what was stored. Documents arriving without those fields belong back at the boundary, because a corpus of unknown origin cannot be un-mixed once it has been indexed. Show the records emitted by one complete run, one per job and one per document batch.

evidenceHint.en: Records emitted by one full pipeline run, showing input and output digests per job and provenance fields per document batch

text.en: Emit input and output digests from each transformation job.
Record the code version and parameters that each job ran with.
Stamp each ingested document with source URI, fetch time and licence.
Reject documents that reach ingestion with no provenance fields.
Backfill tags on corpora already indexed, or flag them unknown.

title.en: Move model-change and labelling records onto append-only storage engineers cannot rewrite

description.en: An audit record an engineer can edit proves only what the last editor wanted it to say. Put the model-change trail - promotions, rollbacks, weight replacements, hyperparameter changes and the approvals behind them - and the labelling ledger into a store with retention locking, then take update and delete rights away from every identity the pipeline runs as, the writer included. Chaining each entry to the digest of the one before it makes a deletion detectable instead of invisible, which matters most in the case where the person covering their tracks owns the pipeline.

evidenceHint.en: Storage configuration plus the denied tamper attempt, alongside the hash chain linking consecutive entries

text.en: Select a store that supports retention locking or WORM.
Strip update and delete grants from the writing identity.
Hash each entry together with the previous entry's digest.
Attempt an edit of a stored record and capture the refusal.
Name who holds break-glass access and what triggers its use.

title.en: Log every labelling decision with the annotator, the guideline revision and the adjudication

description.en: Labels move quietly: an annotator relabels an item, a reviewer overrides it, a second pass re-adjudicates a disagreement, and the dataset that trains the model ends up different from the one anybody signed off. Each of those acts wants its own entry - the item, the label before and after, the person or automated labeller responsible, the guideline revision in force, the moment it happened - and bulk relabelling scripts belong in the same ledger rather than running past it. Where this is missing, a poisoned or mistaken label cannot be traced to the pass that introduced it.

evidenceHint.en: Labelling ledger for the period, one entry per label applied, overridden or re-adjudicated

text.en: Record the item, the previous label and the new label.
Attribute each entry to a person or an automated labeller.
Capture the guideline revision that was in force at the time.
Route bulk relabelling jobs through the same ledger.
Sample a week of entries and confirm no pass is missing.

title.en: Reconcile a released model version against the records its pipeline should have produced

description.en: Pick a version that shipped since the last review and rebuild its history from the stored trail alone - the datasets and transformations that fed it, the label batches applied, the approval and promotion events, the provenance tags on the corpora it retrieves from. Anything that can only be established by asking the engineer who ran it is a hole in the trail rather than a lapse of memory, and it is raised against the pipeline stage that failed to write. Working on a real version also settles whether the append-only store is still readable months after the entries landed.

evidenceHint.en: Reconciliation write-up for the sampled version, listing each missing entry and the stage that owed it

text.en: Select a model version released since the last review.
Rebuild its history from the stored records alone.
Compare that history with what the team remembers doing.
Raise each gap against the pipeline stage that owed the record.
Open an entry from the oldest retained period and read it.

templates.title: C2 Input Validation
templates.description: Implements AISVS-C2: validates what arrives at the model — Unicode normalisation before tokenization, decoding of encoding and representation smuggling, a character allowlist and a context-window ceiling, instruction-hierarchy separation of untrusted content, and injection, many-shot and harmful-content screening across every modality a request carries.
templates.objective: To ensure untrusted content is normalised, decoded and bounded before tokenization, and screened for injection and flooding in every modality a request can carry.
templates.successCriteria:
Every untrusted input path is inventoried with its origin, modality, destination prompt and current checking.
Text reaching the tokenizer is Unicode-normalised, stripped of invisible characters, fully decoded and under the token ceiling.
A planted override inside untrusted content does not displace the system directive above it in the instruction hierarchy.
Rejected inputs are held in both their arriving and normalised form with the screening step that acted on them.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the dated inventory of untrusted input paths, each with its modality and destination prompt.
Collect the sanitiser code path and its unit tests for Unicode form, invisible characters, nested decoding, allowlisted characters and the token ceiling.
Gather the screening configuration: classifiers per modality, blocking and review scores, and unsupported-language behaviour.
Retrieve the period's input-validation decision log and the latest smuggling corpus run report.

Analysis:
Send homoglyph, zero-width and multiply-encoded payloads down each path and read the normalised form recorded.
Plant an override instruction inside untrusted content and confirm the system directive survived it.
Submit a many-shot flooding prompt and check that both the token ceiling and the flooding screen acted.
Review the corpus run for payload families that reached the model and the rule that missed each one.

Output:
A path-by-path sanitisation result placing arriving text beside its normalised form.
An instruction-hierarchy test record showing which directive held.
A corpus run report naming families blocked, families through, and the re-run result after each fix.

title.en: Inventory every untrusted input path that reaches a prompt, with the modality it carries

description.en: Validation gets installed where the product is most visible — the chat box — while retrieved document chunks, tool results, uploaded files, image captions and third-party API responses reach the same tokenizer through code that never calls it. Trace each caller of prompt assembly and write one row per path giving where the content comes from, the modality it arrives as, the prompt it lands in and whatever checking it meets today. Mark the paths carrying text an earlier model turn produced, because that re-enters the window looking like the system's own words. Attach the inventory dated at the point it was compiled.

evidenceHint.en: Dated inventory of input paths: origin, modality, destination prompt and the checking each one meets today

text.en: Trace every caller that assembles a prompt and list the fields it fills.
Record the origin and modality of each field, from end user to retrieved chunk.
Name the validation each path passes through today, or write down none.
Mark paths carrying earlier model output that re-enters a later prompt.
Date the inventory and hand it to the owner of the validation stage.

title.en: Build the pre-tokenizer stage that normalises, decodes and bounds untrusted text

description.en: Everything downstream compares strings whose encoding the sender chose, so this stage runs once, on the single path all prompt assembly goes through, before any tokenizer or classifier sees the text. Normalise to one Unicode form, take out the invisible and direction-changing characters, and decode layered encodings until the text stops changing — a payload wrapped twice in base64 and once in percent-encoding is inert to a screen that decodes a single round. Hold each field to the characters it legitimately needs, rewrite the chat template's own delimiters as literals so a caller cannot open a system turn inside their own message, and take the token count after all of that, refusing an oversized request instead of truncating it into something nobody wrote. Attach the stage's code path with the unit tests covering each rule.

evidenceHint.en: Sanitiser code path plus a unit test per rule: Unicode form, invisible characters, nested decoding, allowlisted character set, delimiter escaping and token ceiling

text.en: Apply one Unicode normalisation form to each untrusted field at assembly.
Remove zero-width, bidirectional and control characters, and fold homoglyphs.
Decode nested encodings until the text stops changing, capping the rounds.
Reject a field carrying characters outside its allowlist rather than stripping them.
Rewrite the chat template's reserved tokens and role markers as literal characters.
Count tokens after normalisation and refuse a request over the context budget.

title.en: Enforce the instruction hierarchy and screen untrusted segments for injection and flooding

description.en: A normalised string is still a string that can say 'ignore the above'. Wrap retrieved and user-supplied content in a segment the system prompt names as data, keep the system directive above anything that segment asserts, and prove it with a test that plants an override inside the data and asserts the directive still governs. Then screen before the call goes out: an injection classifier over each untrusted segment, a ceiling on repeated exemplar pairs so a many-shot flood is caught by its shape rather than its wording, harmful-content categories with the block and review scores written beside them, and a stated outcome — refuse, strip the segment, or send to a person — for each. A language the screen does not cover fails closed instead of passing unscored, non-text attachments get checks of their own, and the request is scored as one whole so a payload split between an image and its caption is not waved through in halves. File the screening configuration with the thresholds and the routing beside each outcome.

evidenceHint.en: Screening configuration: classifiers per modality, the score at which each category blocks or goes to review, the unsupported-language behaviour, and a test showing a system directive surviving a planted override

text.en: Fence retrieved and user text in a segment the system prompt marks as data.
Test that an override written inside that segment leaves the directive intact.
Score each untrusted segment with an injection classifier before the call is made.
Cap repeated exemplar pairs in one request and flag a many-shot flood.
Write the block and review score per harmful category, failing closed on an uncovered language.
Check attached images, audio and documents, then score the request as a single whole.

title.en: Capture each rejected or flagged input in both its raw and normalised form

description.en: Keep one entry for every input the stage rejected, rewrote or let through carrying a suspicion marker, holding the text as it arrived — bytes and encoding intact, stored as an inert literal — beside the text the normaliser produced, and which screening step acted on it. The pair is the whole value: a homoglyph string or a nested base64 wrapper reads as innocent once decoded and as unreadable noise before, so an entry carrying only one side cannot settle whether a real attempt was stopped or a French surname was eaten by the character allowlist. Mark each entry on review as a genuine attempt or a false positive, and let those markings drive the next change to thresholds and allowlists. Without the record the stage's settings can only be argued about, never measured, and the usual outcome is that they are loosened after one loud complaint. Attach the input-validation decision log for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Input-validation decision log for the period: one entry per rejected, sanitised or suspicion-marked input giving the arriving text, the normalised output, the screening step that acted, and the attack-or-false-positive verdict recorded on review

text.en: Keep one entry per input the stage rejected, sanitised or flagged.
Store the arriving text as an inert literal beside its normalised form.
Record which normalisation or screening step made the decision.
Mark each entry on review as a genuine attempt or a false positive.
Carry the false positives into the next tuning of thresholds and allowlists.
Hold the log against the version of the stage that produced it.

title.en: Retest the input-validation stage against a smuggling and injection corpus

description.en: A rule is asserted by the code implementing it and refuted only by input that gets past it, so keep a corpus with a family per rule the stage claims to enforce: homoglyph and zero-width substitution, doubly-encoded payloads, forged role delimiters, context-window floods, many-shot exemplar stacks, and payloads that assemble only when an image and its caption are read together. Fire it at the deployed route rather than a local copy of the sanitiser, since the gap this usually finds is a caller that never invoked the stage at all. Anything reaching the model goes on a list beside the rule that should have caught it, is fixed or knowingly accepted with a reason, and the corpus runs again against the change. Hold the run report with the per-family results for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Corpus run report naming the payload families fired, which reached the model, the rule that missed each one, and the result of the re-run after the fix

text.en: Assemble one payload family per rule the stage claims to enforce.
Add payloads that only work when two modalities are combined.
Fire the corpus at the deployed route, not a local copy of the code.
List every payload that reached the model and the rule that missed it.
Fix or accept each bypass, then run the corpus again against the change.

templates.title: C3 Model Lifecycle Management & Change Control
templates.description: Implements AISVS-C3: keeps an inventory of the model artefacts this organisation has deployed, cryptographically signs the artefacts its own pipeline produces, verifies those signatures at deployment and again at load, and puts every model change through re-testing and a staged rollout that can be reversed to a complete earlier state.
templates.objective: To ensure only signed model artefacts of known provenance serve traffic, and that every model change is re-tested, released in stages and reversible to a complete earlier state.
templates.successCriteria:
Every artefact serving production traces to the build run that produced it, with unidentifiable builds flagged.
Checkpoints and quantised copies are signed as their build stage completes, against published verification keys.
A tampered artefact is refused at deployment admission and again when a process loads the weights.
Candidate builds clear the safety suite and reach production in staged traffic, with a rollback that restores every component.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the dated register of loaded artefacts with digest, build run, environment, endpoint and owning team.
Collect the signing configuration for each pipeline stage and a signature payload binding a digest to its run.
Gather the admission-controller and model-loader verification settings with the refusal log for a tampered artefact.
Retrieve per-release records covering suite results, quantisation re-test and rollout timeline, plus the rollback drill record.

Analysis:
Compare the digests the serving fleet reports against the register and query anything unmatched.
Present an altered artefact at admission and again at load, confirming both points refused it.
Check that a quantised copy was re-tested rather than inheriting its parent build's result.
Read the drill record for components missed on restore and the shared-state findings it raised.

Output:
A fleet-to-register reconciliation naming artefacts that cannot be traced to a build.
A two-point verification result covering admission and load.
A release record per candidate giving suite outcome, rollout stages and the rollback completeness finding.

title.en: Inventory every model artefact serving production traffic and trace each to the run that produced it

description.en: Model artefacts accumulate faster than anyone records them: a base model, three fine-tunes, a quantised copy on the edge fleet, and an adapter somebody loaded for an experiment that never ended. Walk each serving process and read the digest it has actually loaded rather than the version named in the deployment manifest, then write one row per artefact giving that digest, the training or fine-tuning run it came from, the environment it runs in and the team that owns it. A row whose build run cannot be named is the finding this task exists to surface, because nothing later in this control can sign, verify or roll back an artefact whose origin is unknown. Attach the register dated at the point it was compiled.

evidenceHint.en: Dated register of loaded artefacts: digest, build run, environment, serving endpoint and owning team, with unidentifiable builds flagged

text.en: Read the artefact digest each serving process has actually loaded.
Match every digest to the training or fine-tuning run that built it.
Record the environment and endpoint the artefact is serving from.
Add adapters, quantised copies and retained checkpoints as their own rows.
Flag any loaded artefact whose origin nobody can account for.

title.en: Sign each model artefact as its build stage completes, checkpoints and quantised copies included

description.en: Signing only the final release build leaves every earlier hand-off unprotected, and most of a model pipeline is hand-offs: a training run writes a checkpoint, a fine-tune reads it, a quantiser rewrites the weights, a packaging job pushes to the registry. Have each stage sign what it emits over a payload binding the artefact digest to the run identifier and to the input it consumed, so the next stage can tell whether it received what the previous stage produced rather than something swapped in between. Signing keys belong in the KMS or HSM the pipeline authenticates to, never baked into a job image, and the verification material has to be published where deployment and serving can fetch it. Keep one complete signature bundle as evidence of what a stage's payload actually covers.

evidenceHint.en: Signing configuration for each pipeline stage, a sample signature payload binding digest to run, and the published location of the verification keys

text.en: Move the signing keys into the KMS the pipeline authenticates to.
Sign the output of every stage, not only the release build.
Bind the digest, run identifier and input artefact into the payload.
Store each signature beside its artefact in the model registry.
Publish the verification keys where deployment and serving can read them.

title.en: Enforce signature checks at deployment admission and again when a process loads the weights

description.en: A check that runs only at deploy time protects a snapshot of the filesystem, not what the server reads at load: weights get hot-swapped, caches are warmed from another bucket, a sidecar pulls an adapter minutes after the pod was admitted. Put verification in both places and have both fail closed, so an unsigned or altered artefact stops the rollout instead of emitting a warning nobody reads. Narrow the keys production trusts to the release key alone, which is what stops a job in the training environment promoting its own output straight into the serving path. Prove it with a deliberately tampered artefact and capture what the refusal looked like at each point.

evidenceHint.en: Admission-controller and model-loader verification settings, plus the log showing a tampered artefact being refused at both points

text.en: Add the signature check to the deployment admission path.
Verify the digest again inside the model loader before inference starts.
Make both checks fail closed rather than warn and continue.
Limit the production trust store to the release signing key.
Attempt a deploy with a tampered artefact and keep the refusal log.

title.en: Test every candidate build against the safety suite and release it in staged traffic

description.en: A fine-tune, a quantisation or an RLHF pass can quietly restore behaviour the previous build refused, and the parent model's passing scores say nothing about the artefact that will actually serve. Run the suite against the candidate itself, then repeat it after quantisation or any weight conversion, since conversion is precisely where refusals and guardrails get lost. For reinforcement learning runs, pin and verify the base version the run started from and read the reward curves and sampled outputs for specification gaming before anything leaves the pipeline. Traffic then moves in stages with the rollback trigger armed on error, latency and refusal rates, instead of one cut-over that has no observation window.

evidenceHint.en: Per-release record: suite version and results for each candidate, quantisation re-test, RLHF base version and reward review, and the staged rollout timeline

text.en: Run the full safety and security suite against the candidate artefact.
Repeat the same suite after quantisation or any weight conversion.
Record the verified base version each RLHF run started from.
Read reward curves and sampled outputs for specification gaming.
Arm the rollback trigger on error, latency and refusal rates.
Move traffic in stages and record the digest that reached full traffic.

title.en: Exercise a rollback of a live model version and confirm the restored state is complete

description.en: Rollback is the one path here that goes unused until the day it has to work, and a partial restore is the usual outcome: weights revert while the tokenizer, the adapter set, the prompt template, the feature schema or a warm cache stay on the new version, leaving a hybrid nobody has ever tested. Pick a model currently taking traffic, trigger the reversal the way the automated trigger would, and compare every component of the restored deployment against the register row for the version being returned to. While both versions are briefly live, look for state the older one reads that the newer one wrote — cached entries, session memory, embeddings — and close the review by reconciling the register against the digests the serving fleet reports.

evidenceHint.en: Rollback drill record naming each component restored or missed, the shared-state findings, and the reconciliation against what the serving fleet reports

text.en: Pick a version currently serving and trigger its rollback path.
Compare weights, tokenizer, adapters and configuration after the restore.
Check the caches and session state the older version reads from.
Time how long the restore took from trigger to stable traffic.
Reconcile the register against the digests the serving processes report.
Raise a finding for every component that did not come back.

templates.title: C4 Infrastructure, Configuration & Deployment Security
templates.description: Implements AISVS-C4: run model workloads inside isolated sandboxes on attested hardware, restrict the serialization formats a loader will accept, and keep weights protected wherever they execute — cluster accelerators, edge boxes and mobile devices.
templates.objective: To ensure model workloads execute only inside confined sandboxes on attested hardware, and that weights stay protected on cluster accelerators, edge boxes and handsets alike.
templates.successCriteria:
Every runtime, accelerator and device executing a model is registered with its firmware level and confidential-computing capability.
A workload cannot read beyond its own sandbox, and accelerator memory reads back as zero once a job ends.
Loaders accept only signed artefacts in serialization formats that execute no code as they load.
A host or device serves only after its attestation is verified, and jobs are held back where verification fails.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the execution-environment register covering hosts, accelerators, firmware levels and accepted formats.
Collect the per-runtime sandbox profiles and the accelerator partitioning settings in force.
Gather the loader configuration naming accepted formats and signing keys, with a rejected-checkpoint transcript.
Retrieve the period admission record of measured firmware, enclave quotes, verdicts and jobs held back.

Analysis:
Attempt a read outside a workload's sandbox and confirm the runtime denied it.
Read device memory back after a job completes and check it returns zero.
Offer the loader a code-bearing serialization format and confirm it refused to load.
Compare the nodes currently serving against the admission record and query any that served without a verified quote.

Output:
An environment reconciliation naming hosts and devices serving unattested.
A negative-test record listing each forbidden action attempted, the response received, and a ticket where nothing refused.
A memory residue measurement alongside the loader rejection transcript.

title.en: Inventory every runtime, accelerator and device that executes a model

description.en: Start from the deployment manifests rather than from memory: list each service that loads model weights, the host it runs on, the accelerator and firmware level underneath it, whether that host can produce an attestation report, and the artefact formats its loader accepts today. The edge and mobile fleets belong in the same register, because a phone running a downloaded model is an execution environment everything below has to reach. Hardening written without this register lands on the machines somebody happened to remember, while the hosts nobody named keep running unchanged. Attach the register with the date it was compiled.

evidenceHint.en: Execution-environment register giving each host, its accelerator and firmware level, its confidential-computing capability, and the formats its loader accepts

text.en: Walk the deployment manifests and list every service that loads weights.
Record the accelerator model, driver and firmware version of each host.
Mark which hosts can produce a hardware attestation report and which cannot.
Add the edge and mobile fleets, naming who holds each device.
Note, per runtime, the serialization formats its loader accepts today.

title.en: Configure each inference runtime so a workload cannot read beyond its own sandbox

description.en: Give every runtime a profile that states the syscalls it may make, mounts the weights read-only and denies egress to anything outside the allowlisted endpoints, then carry the same discipline down to the accelerator: one tenant per device slice, device memory zeroed between jobs, peer-to-peer links limited to the interconnect topology that was approved. On-device inference gets the same process and memory separation as the fleet. Shared device memory is the leak that leaves no trace in application logs — the next tenant simply reads what the last one left behind, which is why the scrub has to be demonstrated rather than assumed.

evidenceHint.en: Per-runtime sandbox profiles, the accelerator partitioning settings in force, and the residue check showing device memory read back as zero

text.en: Write the syscall and filesystem profile for each inference container.
Mount weights read-only and block egress beyond allowlisted endpoints.
Partition each accelerator so a single tenant holds a device slice.
Zero device memory between jobs and read it back to prove it.
Disable peer links the approved interconnect topology does not list.
Apply the same process separation to on-device inference at the edge.

title.en: Restrict the loader to signed artefacts in formats that execute no code

description.en: Pickle-backed checkpoints run attacker code at the moment of deserialisation, before a single token is generated, so the loader — not a scanner sitting downstream of it — is where the format decision has to be enforced. Set the accepted list, close the paths that rebuild arbitrary objects, convert whatever remains in a rejected format and re-hash it, and make signature verification a precondition of mapping weights into memory. Weights bound for a phone or an edge box travel encrypted under a key the device's secure element holds, and are unwrapped there rather than into a readable file on disk.

evidenceHint.en: Loader configuration naming the accepted formats and signing keys, plus a transcript of a rejected checkpoint failing to load

text.en: Set the accepted format list and reject pickle-backed checkpoints.
Close loader paths that rebuild arbitrary objects during deserialisation.
Convert the artefacts still in a rejected format and re-hash them.
Sign every model build and check it before the weights are mapped in.
Encrypt device-bound weights under a key held in the secure element.
Add a CI test asserting a pickle artefact fails to load.

title.en: Log the attestation result for every node and device admitted to serve a model

description.en: The gate is worth what its record shows: each accelerator's firmware measurement compared against the pinned version, a fresh enclave quote taken before the scheduler places a job, the key that decrypts the weights released only once that quote verifies, and an edge device authenticated by hardware identity before it is allowed to sync. Run it fail-closed and keep the refusals with their reason codes, since an admission gate that has quietly degraded into passing everything looks identical to one that is working until somebody notices no refusal has been written in months.

evidenceHint.en: Admission record for the period: one line per host, its measured firmware and enclave quote, the verdict reached, and the jobs held back

text.en: Pin the firmware version each accelerator model is allowed to run.
Compare the signed firmware measurement against that pin at boot.
Require a fresh enclave quote with memory encryption turned on.
Release the weight-decryption key only when the quote verifies.
Authenticate an edge device by hardware identity before it syncs.
Keep refused admissions for the quarter with their reason codes.

title.en: Retest each restriction by attempting the thing it forbids

description.en: A configuration applied once is not a configuration still in force, and every item above fails silently in the direction that looks healthy. So try the forbidden move each quarter: hand the loader a pickle artefact, offer a node whose firmware has been rolled back, read accelerator memory the instant another tenant's job ends, pull a model file off an edge device and inspect the bytes. Where the system refuses, that refusal is the proof; where it does not, the finding stays open until the setting is corrected and the attempt repeated against the corrected fleet.

evidenceHint.en: Quarterly negative-test record naming each attempt, how the system responded, and the tickets opened where nothing refused

text.en: Hand the loader a pickle artefact and expect a refusal.
Offer a node with rolled-back firmware and watch admission fail.
Read accelerator memory straight after another tenant's job ends.
Pull a model file off an edge device and inspect the bytes.
Open a ticket for every restriction that failed to refuse.
Reconcile the register against what the fleet actually reports.

templates.title: C5 Access Control & Identity for AI Components & Users
templates.description: Implements AISVS-C5: who and what may reach the AI stack, and on whose authority. Covers a fresh authentication challenge before high-risk AI operations, short-lived audience-bound tokens for federated agents, a default-deny allow-list over models, indexes and tools, the end user's entitlements carried into retrieval and output filtering, authorization decided outside the agent that acts on the answer, just-in-time privilege that expires by itself, classification labels travelling to downstream stores, and proof that one tenant's fine-tuning or inference cannot touch or be observed by another.
templates.defaultOwnerHint: Identity and Access Management / AI Platform Engineering
templates.objective: To ensure that access to models, indexes and tools is decided outside the agent that acts on it, on the end user's own entitlements, and never across a tenant boundary.
templates.successCriteria:
Every model, index, tool endpoint and fine-tuning job an identity can reach carries a sensitivity label.
Authorisation is answered outside the agent runtime, denies by default and reads the end user's entitlements.
Agent credentials expire in minutes, bind to one audience, and elevated roles lapse without anyone revoking them.
Per-account query runs return only passages that account is cleared for, and no tenant's work is visible to another.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the dated register of AI resources with its sensitivity labels and high-risk operations.
Collect the policy decision point's configuration, deny default and allow-listed identifiers.
Request the token and elevation policy with one federated agent's issuance trace.
Gather the per-account query run record and the passages returned to each account.
Obtain the tenant isolation write-up for the fine-tuning, cache and batching attempts.

Analysis:
Trace register entries to the allow-list and confirm an unlisted resource identifier is refused, not defaulted open.
Confirm the decision service runs apart from agent runtimes and that no agent writes its own entitlement records.
Check token lifetime, audience and scope, and that an expired token is refused at the resource rather than the client.
Compare the passages each account received against its entitlements, and follow the isolation defects to their fixes.

Output:
A coverage finding on the register against the AI resources production exposes.
An allow-list and deny-default test result with the refusals observed.
A token and elevation conformance summary per agent identity.
A defect list from the retrieval run and the tenant boundary exercise.

title.en: Catalogue the AI resources reachable by identity, with a sensitivity label on each

description.en: The allow-list, the label propagation and the step-up rules all need the same denominator: which models, vector indexes, tool endpoints, fine-tuning jobs and data stores an identity can reach, and how sensitive each one is. Without that list the allow-list gets written from memory, and the resource nobody wrote down keeps its implicit permission. Cover human users, service accounts and the federated agents that call on a user's behalf, and mark the operations treated as high-risk. Attach the register.

evidenceHint.en: Register of AI resources carrying a sensitivity label, the identities that reach each one and the operations marked high-risk

text.en: List the models, vector indexes, tool endpoints and fine-tuning jobs an identity can call.
Record the human, service and agent identities holding access to each entry.
Apply the classification label the resource inherits from its source data.
Mark the operations a caller may run only after re-authenticating.

title.en: Configure the authorization decision to be made outside the agent that acts on it

description.en: Route every resource and tool call an agent makes to a policy decision point that the agent's own process cannot read or rewrite, answer deny unless the target appears on the allow-list, and decide on the calling end user's entitlements rather than the agent's service identity. An agent that evaluates its own permissions can be argued into granting them, and a retrieval layer running as a privileged service account hands back documents the person asking was never cleared to see. Record the deny default and the decision path in the design note attached here.

evidenceHint.en: Design note and policy configuration showing the separated decision point, the deny default and the end-user context carried per call

text.en: Stand up the policy decision point as a service separate from agent runtimes.
Set the default answer to deny and admit only listed resource identifiers.
Pass the calling end user's entitlements with each retrieval and tool request.
Block agent processes from writing their own policy or entitlement records.
Test that an unlisted resource identifier is refused rather than defaulted open.

title.en: Issue federated agents short-lived tokens and time-boxed privilege

description.en: An agent identity should hold a credential that dies in minutes, is bound to one audience and carries only the scopes its current task needs, with anything more privileged granted as an elevation that ends by itself. A long-lived agent secret lifted from a log or coaxed out of a prompt is a permanent foothold, and a standing administrator role on an AI platform is exactly what an injected instruction reaches for. Wire the operations marked high-risk during scoping to a fresh authentication challenge. The token policy and a sample issuance trace are the evidence.

evidenceHint.en: Token and elevation policy with an issuance trace showing lifetime, audience, scopes and the expiry of a granted elevation

text.en: Set token lifetime and audience binding for each agent identity.
Replace any static agent secret with a credential minted per run.
Grant privileged roles through a request that expires without manual revocation.
Require a fresh authentication challenge before a high-risk operation executes.
Confirm an expired token is rejected by the resource, not merely by the client.

title.en: Run a per-account query set through retrieval and the output filter

description.en: Take a fixed set of questions whose answers sit in documents only some accounts may see, ask them as each account in turn, and write down what came back. Nothing else catches an index rebuilt without its access metadata, a label that quietly stopped travelling to a downstream cache, or a filter that lets a restricted passage through inside a summary. Finish by looking for the sensitive values the run retrieved in conversation history, caches and logs, where they should no longer be. Keep the run record with the accounts used and the answers returned.

evidenceHint.en: Run record listing each account used, the questions asked, the passages returned and where filtering intervened

text.en: Build the question set from documents with known, differing audiences.
Ask every question as each account and capture the raw response.
Compare the returned passages against that account's entitlements.
Search caches, logs and history for the sensitive values just retrieved.
Raise a defect for any passage returned outside its label's audience.

title.en: Exercise the tenant boundary on shared training and inference infrastructure

description.en: Tenants share accelerators, caches and one fine-tuning pipeline, so the separation has to be demonstrated rather than credited to the scheduler. Fine-tune for a single tenant and check that no other tenant's adapter, dataset or evaluation score moved; then hunt the inference path for a prompt cache entry served across tenants, a batched response carrying a neighbour's content, or timing that reveals another tenant's activity. Isolation that held at design time fails silently after a capacity change nobody flagged as a security change. Write up each attempt with its result and the fix raised where one gave way.

evidenceHint.en: Isolation test write-up covering fine-tuning cross-effects, shared-cache and batching observations, and the defects it produced

text.en: Fine-tune a model for one tenant on the shared pipeline.
Check another tenant's adapters, datasets and eval scores for movement.
Probe whether a prompt cache entry is served across tenant boundaries.
Inspect batched inference responses for content belonging to another tenant.
File a fix for every boundary that let something across.

templates.title: C6 Supply Chain Security for Models
templates.description: Implements AISVS-C6: governs the model artefacts this organisation acquires rather than builds. Imported weights, adapters, tokenizers and inference images are fetched only from sources somebody has ruled on, scanned for executable payloads before anything serving can load them, and pinned to a recorded hash so a third-party artefact stays verifiable long after the download; an adopted upstream version is behaviourally tested before it leaves development, and every release emits a signed, machine-readable AI BOM whose build stops when a component's metadata is incomplete.
templates.objective: To ensure that model weights, adapters, tokenizers and inference images obtained from outside are judged, scanned and pinned before any serving system can load them.
templates.successCriteria:
Every imported artefact is recorded against its publisher, its fetch location and a ruling on that source.
Nothing reaches a serving system until a serialisation-aware scan has cleared it and its hash is on record.
Each release emits a signed bill of materials, and a build carrying a blank component field stops.
An adopted upstream version is put through the behavioural baseline before it leaves development.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the dated import catalogue of artefacts the organisation acquired rather than trained.
Collect the import gate configuration together with the quarantine scan log for the period.
Request the signed AI bill of materials from the latest release and the build log behind it.
Gather the promotion reports naming the digest exercised and the probes run against it.
Obtain the reconciliation of files loaded on production inference hosts.

Analysis:
Check each row names the publisher's own fetch location, and single out artefacts that came by mirror or re-upload.
Verify the scan log gives a verdict, scanner version and hash for everything admitted, and names what stopped each rejection.
Trace bill-of-materials entries back to catalogue rows, and confirm the build log shows an incomplete entry halting a run.
Read the promotion reports for trigger and refusal probes, then match production's loaded files to a BOM entry and hash.

Output:
An exception list of unruled and mirror-sourced import sources.
A scan and digest coverage figure against the artefacts admitted in the period.
An assessment of bill-of-materials completeness and signature validity for the release examined.
A register of production artefacts matching no bill-of-materials entry, with their disposition.

title.en: Catalogue every model artefact the organisation imports rather than trains, and the source it arrived from

description.en: Go through the serving stack and write down each set of weights, adapter, tokenizer, embedding model and inference image that came from outside, one row apiece, naming the publisher, the precise place it was fetched from and the revision pinned. Once a file is sitting on disk, a download from a vendor's own registry and one from an anonymous re-upload are indistinguishable, so the fetch location has to be captured while somebody still knows it. Rule on each source as the row is written, rather than leaving a list of URLs nobody has judged. Attach the dated catalogue.

evidenceHint.en: Dated import catalogue giving each externally obtained artefact, its upstream publisher, the exact fetch location and the approval ruling on that source

text.en: Walk the model registry, serving images and dependency manifests for weights nobody here trained.
Record the upstream project, the exact URL or registry fetched from, and the version or revision pinned.
Mark the artefacts that arrived through a mirror, proxy or third-party re-upload rather than the publisher.
Rule on each source as approved, approved with conditions, or not approved for import, and write why.
Date the catalogue and hold it as the source list the import gate is configured against.

title.en: Scan each incoming artefact for executable payloads and pin the digest it was admitted under

description.en: Serialised model formats execute code the moment they are loaded, so an artefact that opens cleanly in a notebook has not been checked — it has been run. Stand up an import path that holds arriving files in quarantine, examines them for embedded scripts and unsafe deserialisation before any serving system can reach them, and writes down the hash of whatever passed. That hash is what keeps a third-party artefact verifiable afterwards: without it nobody can say whether the weights in production are the ones the scanner cleared. The evidence is the gate configuration together with the quarantine log for the period.

evidenceHint.en: Import gate configuration plus the quarantine scan log showing the verdict, scanner version and recorded hash for everything admitted

text.en: Route every import into a quarantine area no serving system is able to read from.
Run a serialisation-aware scanner over the file, covering pickle opcodes and embedded scripts.
Record the SHA-256 of each admitted file alongside the scan verdict and the scanner version used.
Capture any upstream signature, provenance attestation or published checksum and store it beside that hash.
Re-check the stored hash on every load of the artefact and fail the load when it differs.
Log the rejected imports, naming the finding that stopped each one at the quarantine boundary.

title.en: Build the release stage that emits a signed AI BOM and rejects components with missing metadata

description.en: A bill of materials typed up after a release describes what somebody remembered, and the customer who asks which third-party model shipped gets an answer no one can check. Wire the generation into the pipeline so the document falls out of the build itself, stop the run when a component's version, source or licence field is blank, and sign the result so a reader can tell it came from the pipeline and not from a text editor. Blank fields are the failure mode worth designing against: they accumulate silently and each one hides a component whose origin is now unknown. Attach the signed document and the build log from the release it describes.

evidenceHint.en: Pipeline definition and the signed bill of materials from the latest release, with a build log showing an incomplete entry stopping the run

text.en: Choose a machine-readable BOM format and list the fields every AI component must carry.
Emit the document from the release pipeline itself instead of assembling it by hand afterwards.
Fail the build where a model, dataset, adapter or library entry leaves a required field empty.
Sign the finished document with the release key before any artefact is published from that run.
Commit each signed copy to version control under the release tag that it describes.

title.en: Test every adopted upstream version against the behavioural baseline before it leaves development

description.en: Scanning proves no code runs on load; it says nothing whatever about what the weights do once they are loaded. Each time an upstream version is taken up, put that exact artefact through the probe suite in development — trigger phrases, refusal behaviour, task quality — and set the results beside what the version currently in service scored. Publishers re-train and republish under a tag that has not changed, so a model that behaved well a month ago is no evidence about the file pulled this morning. Hand in the report produced for each promotion made in the period.

evidenceHint.en: Per-promotion test report naming the digest exercised, the probes run and the comparison drawn against the version currently serving

text.en: Exercise the agreed probe suite against the candidate artefact, naming its digest in the run.
Cover backdoor triggers and weakened refusals, not task accuracy on its own.
Compare each result with the baseline held for the version presently in service.
Hold the promotion out of development until somebody has read and signed off the report.
File the report against the artefact record so the next adoption has something to compare with.

title.en: Reconcile the artefacts loaded on production inference hosts against the signed BOM and approved sources

description.en: An import gate only sees what passes through it, and an engineer copying weights straight onto a GPU host leaves no trace in the catalogue at all. Take what production has actually loaded and try to match each file against a bill-of-materials entry and the hash captured at import; anything that matches nothing entered outside the control, and surfacing it is the point of the pass. Use the same sweep to ask whether the sources still listed as approved deserve to be — a project that changed hands or moved to a new host is no longer the source that was judged. Attach the reconciliation, including the disposition of everything that matched nothing.

evidenceHint.en: Reconciliation record listing each loaded file, the bill-of-materials entry and hash it matched, and the disposition of everything unmatched

text.en: List the model files and images currently loaded on production inference hosts.
Match each one to a BOM entry and to the hash captured when it was imported.
Investigate anything matching nothing and establish how it reached the host.
Re-check that every source in the catalogue is still approved and still the publisher's own.
Write down what was removed, re-imported or escalated as a result of this pass.

templates.title: C7 Model Behavior, Output Control & Safety Assurance
templates.description: Implements AISVS-C7: governs what the model emits — a schema, length and termination contract for every response surface, egress scanning for leaked context, hidden payloads and call-out markup, citations that resolve to the retrieved chunk plus provenance marks on generated media, and confidence-based holds that stop unreliable or policy-flagged answers reaching the caller.
templates.objective: To ensure that generated content leaves the system only within a stated contract, free of leaked context and active markup, and traceable to the source it claims.
templates.successCriteria:
Each surface emitting generated content has a declared type, length ceiling and stop condition.
Malformed or runaway generations are replaced by the declared fallback rather than delivered.
No released response carries a prompt canary, an encoded payload or remote-loading markup.
Claims drawn from retrieval resolve to the chunk behind them, and generated media is marked.
Answers under the surface threshold are held, and flagged ones await a named approver.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the response-surface catalogue with the contract recorded against each surface.
Collect the schema file for each response type and the validator's rejection log.
Request the egress filter configuration and the blocked-response samples kept for the period.
Gather a worked answer with its citations and a media file said to carry a provenance mark.
Obtain the period register of held and escalated answers with the reviewer decisions.

Analysis:
Compare the catalogue with the endpoints, channels and tool results production returns, and list surfaces holding no contract.
Confirm the rejection log shows a malformed response and one stopped at its ceiling, each replaced by that surface's fallback.
Submit encoded, zero-width and homoglyph text, then follow the worked answer's citations to the chunk each one names.
Re-score a sample of the period's answers against correctness and judge whether threshold moves followed that evidence.

Output:
A list of response surfaces operating without a declared contract.
Validator and egress filter test results, naming any payload that got through.
A citation resolution rate for the answers sampled, with the media mark read.
An opinion on threshold calibration supported by the held-answer outcomes reviewed.

title.en: Catalogue each response surface and the output contract it must meet

description.en: Find every place model-generated content leaves the system — chat replies, JSON returned to another service, tool-call results, generated files and media — and write down what each one is allowed to emit: the response type, its maximum length, the condition that ends generation, whether the answer owes citations, and how much harm a wrong or unsafe answer would do there. A surface nobody has written down is a surface shipped without a limit, and a filter can only be applied where somebody named the exit. Attach the catalogue.

evidenceHint.en: Response-surface catalogue giving the emitted type, length ceiling, stop condition, citation duty and harm rating for each

text.en: List every endpoint, channel and tool result that returns generated content.
Record the response type each surface emits and the format its consumer parses.
Set a maximum output length and an explicit stop condition per surface.
Mark the surfaces that answer from retrieval and therefore owe citations.
Rate the harm a wrong or unsafe answer would cause on each surface.
Name the team accountable for each surface and date the catalogue.

title.en: Enforce the response schema, length ceiling and stop condition at egress

description.en: Turn the contract into code that runs on the way out: each generated response is parsed against a machine-checkable schema for its type, generation halts at the token ceiling and the declared stop sequences, and anything failing either check is replaced by the surface's fallback rather than passed on. Downstream services parse model output as though it were an API response, so one stray sentence wrapped around a JSON object becomes a parse error in somebody else's system, and a generation that never terminates spends a page and a budget at once. Evidence is the schema set plus the rejection log the validator writes.

evidenceHint.en: Schema file per response type with validator rejection logs showing malformed and runaway generations stopped before delivery

text.en: Write a machine-checkable schema for each response type the catalogue names.
Validate every generated response against its schema before it is returned.
Cap output tokens per surface and configure the stop sequences that end it.
Terminate a stream that passes its length ceiling or its time budget.
Return the declared fallback when a check fails, never the raw generation.
Log each rejection with the request identifier and the rule that fired.

title.en: Scan outbound responses for leaked context, hidden payloads and active markup

description.en: Run the safety pass over the finished response rather than over what went in. It needs a harmful-content classifier, a match against system-prompt canaries and internal field names, a decode of base64, zero-width and homoglyph text so the filters read what the consumer will see, and removal of markup whose rendering would make a browser or client fetch a remote resource. A reply carrying an image tag pointed at an attacker's host exfiltrates the conversation the instant it renders, and text a filter cannot read is text no filter was applied to. Keep the blocked-response samples as proof the pass fires.

evidenceHint.en: Egress filter configuration plus blocked-response samples covering harmful text, canary leakage, encoded content and call-out markup

text.en: Run a harmful-content classifier over each response before release.
Match responses against system-prompt canaries and internal field names.
Decode base64, zero-width and homoglyph text before the filters read it.
Remove image sources, auto-loading links and frames from rendered output.
Replace a blocked response with the refusal text and alert the on-call.

title.en: Cite the retrieved chunk behind every claim and mark generated media

description.en: Make trust in an answer checkable by whoever reads it. Carry the document identifier, version and chunk offset out of the retriever so attribution comes from retrieval metadata rather than from whatever the model wrote, link each substantive claim to the passage supporting it, refuse to release a retrieval-backed answer whose citations resolve to nothing, and embed a durable provenance mark in images, audio and video the system generates. Asked for its sources, a model will invent plausible ones, and an unmarked synthetic image is indistinguishable from a photograph once it leaves the product. Hand over a worked answer with resolved citations and a marked media file.

evidenceHint.en: Worked answer showing each claim linked to the source chunk it came from, alongside a media file carrying its provenance mark

text.en: Carry document id, version and chunk offset out of the retriever.
Build each citation from retrieval metadata, not from model text.
Link every substantive claim to the passage that supports it.
Block a retrieval-backed answer whose citations resolve to nothing.
Embed a provenance mark in generated images, audio and video.
Show an AI-generated label beside the media inside the product.

title.en: Score answer reliability and route weak or high-risk replies before release

description.en: Operate the hallucination check as a recurring act rather than a launch-day setting. Every answer carries a confidence estimate built from retrieval overlap and model signals, answers under the threshold for their surface are held and the fallback goes out instead, and answers a policy rule flags as high-risk wait for a named human to approve them. Then test the estimate against reality on a sample of the period's traffic: a threshold calibrated once drifts as the model, the index and the questions change, and a confidence number nobody has compared with correctness is decoration. The period's register of holds, escalations and decisions is the output.

evidenceHint.en: Period register of held and escalated answers listing scores, reviewer decisions and any threshold change they caused

text.en: Attach a confidence estimate to every answer the system produces.
Hold answers under the surface threshold and return the fallback.
Queue policy-flagged high-risk answers for a named human to approve.
Sample the period's answers and compare scores against correctness.
Move a threshold that the sample shows is passing wrong answers.
Record every hold, escalation and decision in the period register.

templates.title: C8 Memory, Embeddings & Vector Database Security
templates.description: Implements AISVS-C8: keeps embeddings, RAG indices and agent memory isolated per tenant — vector identifiers unique within a tenant, document metadata frozen once written, content masked and screened before it is vectorized, and every retrieval confined to live, in-scope rows with expiry and erasure honoured at query time.
templates.objective: To ensure that embeddings and agent memory stay confined to the tenant owning them and that retrieval returns only live, in-scope content that passed the ingestion gate.
templates.successCriteria:
Every embedding and memory store has a named owner, a tenant key and a known identifier scheme.
The store itself refuses a colliding vector identifier and any tag edit made after insert.
Content is masked and screened before embedding, with outliers held where retrieval cannot read them.
Expired vectors, erased subjects and quarantined rows appear in no result set.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the register of embedding and memory stores, evaluation copies included.
Collect the schema migration carrying the tenant-scoped uniqueness constraint and immutable tags.
Request the ingestion configuration and a sample run showing a masked field and a held outlier.
Gather the query-layer filter code with the saved lookup replayed after expiry and erasure.
Obtain the period's cross-tenant probe report with the row identifiers each query returned.

Analysis:
Check the register against the vector stores actually deployed and mark collections holding rows for more than one tenant.
Read the refused-write output to confirm a duplicate identifier and a tag edit were rejected by the store, not the client.
Establish whether masking precedes the embedding call and whether expiry is a query predicate rather than a sweeper's job.
Verify the probes ran against the deployed configuration and follow every unexpected hit to the ticket raised with its owner.

Output:
A gap list naming collections with no recorded identifier scheme or tenant key.
Uniqueness and immutability test results with the refusals captured.
An assessment of the pre-vectorization gate across masking, screening and quarantine.
A cross-tenant probe outcome with the leakage defects still open.

title.en: Inventory every vector collection, its tenant key and its identifier scheme

description.en: Find every store holding embeddings or agent memory — the production vector database, per-team indices, caches that outlive a session, and any evaluation copy carrying real documents — and record for each how a vector identifier is formed, who supplies it, which tenants own rows in it, what metadata travels with each vector, and whether an expiry timestamp is written at all. What usually surfaces here is one collection shared by several customers with the identifier chosen by the ingesting client, which is the condition the rest of this control assumes has been found. Attach the register.

evidenceHint.en: Register of embedding and memory stores, one row per collection, naming its owner, where identifiers come from and which metadata fields are carried

text.en: List every store holding embeddings, evaluation copies included.
Record how each collection forms a vector id and who supplies it.
Name the metadata fields written alongside each vector.
Mark the collections whose rows belong to more than one tenant.
Note which collections write an expiry timestamp and which do not.

title.en: Enforce tenant-scoped vector identifiers and write-once document metadata

description.en: Make the store itself refuse the two writes that break isolation: an identifier that collides with another tenant's row, and an edit to the metadata a document was admitted with. A composite uniqueness constraint over tenant plus identifier stops a caller overwriting a neighbour's vector by guessing an id, and classification, source and tenant tags that reject modification after insert stop a re-ingest job quietly rewriting the very field the retrieval filter later trusts. Corrections then arrive as a fresh vector with its own id while the superseded row is tombstoned.

evidenceHint.en: Schema migration together with failing-write output showing a colliding insert and a tag edit both refused

text.en: Add a uniqueness constraint over tenant plus vector identifier.
Derive the tenant portion from the caller's token, not the payload.
Reject writes aimed at a namespace the caller does not own.
Make classification, source and tenant tags immutable after insert.
Re-ingest a correction as a new vector and tombstone the old row.
Attempt a duplicate id and a tag edit; keep both refusals.

title.en: Build the pre-vectorization gate that masks, screens and quarantines new content

description.en: Everything on its way into the index passes one gate, whatever wrote it. The gate masks fields that must never become an embedding — account numbers, credentials, special-category personal data — before text reaches the embedding model, screens that text for instruction-shaped and retrieval-manipulation phrasing, scores the resulting vector against the collection's existing distribution, and compares the claims it carries against what is already stored so a contradiction is surfaced instead of silently merged. Memory an agent wrote about its own run takes the same path as an uploaded document: trusting it because it came from inside is how a poisoned fact becomes permanent. Anything held goes to a quarantine store the retrieval path cannot read.

evidenceHint.en: Ingestion pipeline configuration plus a sample run showing a masked field, a held outlier and a flagged contradiction

text.en: Mask secrets and identifying fields before the embedding call.
Screen incoming text for instruction-shaped and injected phrasing.
Score each new vector against the collection's existing distribution.
Divert outliers and flagged text into an unreadable quarantine store.
Compare new claims with stored ones and flag the contradictions.
Send agent-written memory through the same gate as uploaded files.

title.en: Restrict what a retrieval may return to live, in-scope vectors

description.en: A retrieval is the moment isolation either holds or does not, so the constraint belongs in the query the store executes and not in a prompt asking the model to ignore rows it should never have received. Assemble the filter from the caller's authenticated scope, refuse any query arriving without one, and evaluate expiry as a predicate inside the query rather than leaving it to a sweeper that may not have run — an expired vector still in the index is an expired vector still returned. This layer is also where erasure becomes real: once a subject's memory is reset, their vectors stop appearing, and quarantined or tombstoned rows appear to nobody.

evidenceHint.en: Query-layer filter code with before-and-after results of one saved lookup run against an expired row, an erased subject and a held item

text.en: Build the query filter from the caller's token, not the prompt.
Refuse any lookup that arrives without a tenant scope attached.
Evaluate the expiry timestamp inside the query predicate itself.
Keep quarantined and tombstoned rows out of every result set.
Add a reset that erases a subject's memory and its derived vectors.
Replay a saved lookup after erasure and confirm nothing returns.

title.en: Run the cross-tenant probe set against the live index each period

description.en: Query the deployed index the way an attacker would and keep what came back. The probe set holds a seeded marker document per tenant, an expired vector, an erased subject's memory and a quarantined item; passing means none of them appears in another tenant's results. Point it at the running configuration rather than a fixture, because a test that supplies its own filter reads green even after a hotfix switched the real one off. Any probe that returns a row it should not goes to the collection's owner with the retrieval trace attached.

evidenceHint.en: Probe report listing every query issued, the row identifiers it returned and the tickets raised for hits that should not have happened

text.en: Seed a marker document into each tenant's collection.
Query with one tenant's credentials for another tenant's markers.
Probe for an expired vector and an erased subject's memory.
Confirm quarantined rows appear in none of the result sets.
Record the identifiers returned beside each probe issued.
Raise every unexpected hit with the team owning the collection.

templates.title: C9 Orchestration & Agentic Security
templates.description: Implements AISVS-C9: keeps agent workflows inside limits somebody actually set — a quota and a timeout on every tool call, a ceiling on what one run may spend, an approval gate in front of actions that cannot be undone, scoped delegation between agents, and a kill-switch that stops a whole swarm from outside the platform it runs on.
templates.objective: To ensure that an agent run stays inside limits somebody set: bounded in calls, time and spend, haltable on demand, and irreversible only on a human release.
templates.successCriteria:
Every workflow in which a model picks its own tool calls is rated for reversibility, call by call and chain by chain.
The runtime turns away a call that passes its quota, timeout or spend ceiling and withdraws that tool from the run.
An irreversible action proceeds only on a release bound to the parameters shown in full to a named approver.
A stop triggered out of band brings every agent in the swarm to a halt within a measured time.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the workflow catalogue listing the tools each run can reach and their reversibility ratings.
Collect the per-tool and per-run limit configuration with a log extract of a call turned away.
Request the approval gate configuration and a worked release record for an irreversible action.
Gather the stop-exercise record with the elapsed time to the last agent ceasing work.
Obtain the periodic reconciliation of agent credentials, delegations and consumption.

Analysis:
Check that each chain carries the worst rating among its steps and that workflows able to edit their own tools are flagged.
Confirm the logged refusal came from the runtime rather than a warning, and that a tool breaching a limit left the run.
Inspect the release record for untruncated parameters, a binding to that one request, and a credential kept out of context.
Read the stop timing and the out-of-band attempt, then set consumption and delegated scopes against each recorded ceiling.

Output:
A completeness view of the workflow catalogue against the agent runs in production.
Enforcement evidence for quotas, timeouts and spend ceilings, with the refusals observed.
An approval gate assessment covering the expired-window case.
A stop capability timing result alongside the delegation and credential findings.

title.en: Catalogue each agent workflow and rate its tool calls by reversibility

description.en: Quotas, gates and budgets get set for a population somebody had to enumerate first, and an agent able to edit its own prompt or add its own tools belongs on that list before anything else is decided. For every workflow where a model picks the next action, write down the tools it may reach, what a call creates or destroys, and whether the effect can be undone. A chain of three harmless steps ending in a payment is a payment; rate the chain by its worst step, not its first. The catalogue is the attachment.

evidenceHint.en: Workflow catalogue: the tools reachable from each run, the effect of every call, its reversibility rating, and the rating carried by each chain

text.en: List every workflow in which a model chooses and invokes tools without a person deciding each step.
Record the tools each workflow may reach and what a single call creates, changes or destroys.
Rate each call reversible, recoverable or irreversible, and name who decided the rating.
Carry the worst rating in a chain onto the whole chain, including calls a sub-agent makes.
Mark the workflows able to alter their own instructions, tool set or code.

title.en: Set a call quota, a timeout and a spend ceiling on every tool an agent invokes

description.en: A limit written in a design document is not a limit; the runtime has to be the thing that refuses. Without one, a looping agent retries the same tool ten thousand times overnight, a slow call holds a worker until the queue backs up, and nobody learns the cost until the invoice arrives. Give each tool a manifest stating the privileges and ceilings it runs under, run it with nothing but the credentials that one tool needs, and make a breach end the tool's participation rather than raise a note. What gets attached is the configuration together with a log line showing a real call turned away.

evidenceHint.en: Per-tool and per-run limit configuration, plus log extracts showing one call refused at a ceiling and one tool withdrawn mid-run

text.en: Give each tool a call quota, a wall-clock timeout and a cap on concurrent invocations.
Cap each execution on tokens, currency spent and total actions before the run is halted.
State the privileges and ceilings of every tool in its manifest, and refuse whatever exceeds them.
Confine each tool to a sandbox holding only its own credentials and an allow-list of reachable destinations.
Validate every tool response against its declared schema and discard the responses that fail.
Withdraw a tool from the run automatically the moment it breaches a declared limit.

title.en: Build the gate that holds an irreversible action until a named person releases it

description.en: An approver shown a truncated parameter list rubber-stamps whatever was hidden, and an approval that is not bound to the exact parameters can be replayed against a different call. Route everything rated irreversible through a gate that shows the full request, ties the release to that request alone, and keeps the approving credential somewhere the agent cannot read — an approval secret sitting in the model's context is an agent approving itself. Where the approver does not answer in time, the action fails rather than proceeds. Hand over the gate configuration with one worked example.

evidenceHint.en: Gate configuration and a worked release record showing the parameters displayed, the approver, the binding to that request, and one action failed on an expired window

text.en: Route every action rated irreversible into the gate before any of it executes.
Show the approver the complete parameters of the pending call, untruncated and unsummarised.
Tie each release cryptographically to those parameters so it cannot free a different call.
Keep approving credentials outside the agent runtime and out of the model's context window.
Fail the action when the approval window closes rather than letting it through unreleased.
Bound what an agent may change about its own instructions, tools or code without a release.

title.en: Exercise the swarm kill-switch and time how long the last agent takes to stop

description.en: A stop control that has never been pulled is a belief, not a capability, and one reachable only through the orchestration platform is unreachable during the incident it exists for. Pull it against a workflow that is genuinely running: measure the gap between the decision and the last agent falling silent, then pull it again over the out-of-band route with the platform console treated as unavailable. Tool calls already in flight when the stop landed are the interesting part — write down which of them completed anyway and what state they left behind.

evidenceHint.en: Stop-exercise record: who triggered it, elapsed time to the final agent ceasing work, the out-of-band attempt, in-flight calls that still completed, and any procedure step found wrong

text.en: Trigger the stop against a multi-agent workflow that is running real work.
Measure the elapsed time from the trigger to the last agent ceasing to act.
Repeat the trigger over the out-of-band route while treating the platform console as unavailable.
Record which in-flight tool calls completed after the stop was issued and what they left behind.
Note every step of the written procedure that behaved differently from how it reads.

title.en: Reconcile agent identities, downstream delegations and what runs actually consumed

description.en: Agents sharing one service account cannot be told apart after the fact, and a sub-agent handed the caller's full token quietly inherits privileges its own work never justified. Once a quarter, take the catalogue and test it against the live estate: whose credential signed which action, whether the requesting run can still be traced from a finished action, how wide the tokens passed downstream turned out to be, and whether the ceilings set earlier match what the runs consumed. Ceilings nobody approaches are theatre; ceilings hit weekly were set wrong.

evidenceHint.en: Reconciliation write-up covering credentials per agent, traced action samples, delegation scopes found, rotations performed, and consumption against each ceiling

text.en: Check that each agent authenticates with a credential of its own rather than a shared account.
Trace a sample of completed actions back to the run and the agent that requested them.
Confirm the token handed to a sub-agent carries narrower scope than the caller's own.
Rotate the agent credentials that are due and withdraw those of workflows now retired.
Compare tokens, spend and call counts consumed against the ceilings recorded for each tool.
Search recent tool parameters and prompts for secrets that were never meant to appear there.
